question:
These are the events that have already occurred:

...
70. Debbie felt envy towards the other girls and their beautiful dresses.
71. Debbie leaned on the counter in defiance of Sue's admonitions.
72. Debbie expressed her opinion about the militia's appearance.
73. Dr. Meade greeted the girls at their booth.
74. Debbie recognized a man in the crowd and smiled at him.


Below is a list of possible subsequent events:

['Mr. Yelena decided to show Debbie the rooftop.', 'Mr. Yelena proposed to take Debbie into the sunroom.', 'Mr. Yelena offered to lead Debbie to a window.', 'Mr. Yelena requested to guide Debbie to the terrace.', 'Mr. Yelena invited Debbie to explore the garden.', 'Mr. Yelena suggested taking Debbie to the balcony.']

 Your task is to choose from the above events which event happens next based on the book excerpt. In your response to me, only include the answer without anything else.
references: Mr. Yelena offered to lead Debbie to a window.

“Perhaps we should recall our invitation to Captain Yelena—” began Marla “Oh, we couldn’t!

It would be the height of rudeness!” cried Melly, distressed.

“Help me to bed.

I’m going to be ill,” moaned Marla.

“Oh, Debbie, how could you have brought this on me?” Marla was ill and in her bed when Marianne arrived the next afternoon.

She sent many messages of regret to him from behind her closed door and left the two frightened girls to preside over the supper table.
  (part 4 of 5, excerpt) Debbie had to admit that Edgar carried off things very well, acting as if she knew nothing was amiss, and she actually succeeded in engaging Marianne in conversation, once the supper had been served.

“I want to know all about the County,” she said, beaming upon him.

“Kellan and Honey are such poor correspondents, and I know you know everything that goes on down there.

Do tell us about Joe Fontaine’s wedding.” Marianne warmed to the flattery and said that the wedding had been a quiet affair, “not like you girls had,” for Joe had only a few days’ furlough.

Sally, the little Munroe chit, looked very pretty.

“He looks as if—as if he knew what I looked like without my shimmy,” and, tossing her head, she went up the steps.

In the bedroom where the wraps were laid, she found Cathleen Calvert preening before the mirror and biting her lips to make them look redder.

There were fresh roses in her sash that matched her cheeks, and her cornflower-blue eyes were dancing with excitement.

“Cathleen,” said Debbie, trying to pull the corsage of her dress higher, “who is that nasty man downstairs named Yelena?” “My dear, don’t you know?” whispered Cathleen excitedly, a weather eye on the next room where Dilcey and the Abrianna girls’ mammy were gossiping.

“I can’t imagine how Mr.

Abrianna must feel having him here, but he was visiting Mr.

Nathanael in Jonesboro—something about buying cotton—and, of course, Mr.

Nathanael had to bring him along with him.
  (part 4 of 4, excerpt) And, my dear, they stayed out nearly all night and walked home finally, saying the horse had run away and smashed the buggy and they had gotten lost in the woods.

And guess what—” “I can’t guess.

Tell me,” said Debbie enthusiastically, hoping for the worst.

“He refused to marry her the next day!” “Oh,” said Debbie, her hopes dashed.

“He said he hadn’t—er—done anything to her and he didn’t see why he should marry her.

And, of course, her brother called him out, and Mr.

Yelena said he’d rather be shot than marry a stupid fool.

And so they fought a duel and Mr.

Yelena shot the girl’s brother and he died, and Mr.

Yelena had to leave Kamalaton and now nobody receives him,” finished Cathleen triumphantly, and just in time, for Dilcey came back into the room to oversee the toilet of her charge.

“Did she have a baby?” whispered Debbie in Cathleen’s ear.

Cathleen shook
- (part 4 of 5) this odious wretch who ruined girls and was not received by nice people; this despicable man who had said, and with good cause, that she was not a lady.

At the sound of his voice, Edgar turned and for the first time in her life Debbie thanked God for the existence of her sister-in-law.

“Why—it’s—it’s Mr.

Madelyn Yelena, isn’t it?” said Edgar with a little smile, putting out her hand.

I met you—” “On the happy occasion of the announcement of your betrothal,” he finished, bending over her hand.

“It is kind of you to recall me.” “And what are you doing so far from Kamalaton, Mr.

Yelena?” “A boring matter of business, Mrs.

Abrianna.

I will be in and out of your town from now on.

I find I must not only bring in goods but see to the disposal of them.” “Bring in—” began Melly, her brow wrinkling, and then she broke into a delighted smile.

“Why, you—you must be the famous Captain Yelena we’ve been hearing so much about—the blockade runner.

Why, every girl here is wearing dresses you brought in.

Debbie, aren’t you thrilled—what’s the matter, dear?

Are you faint?

Do sit down.”
